title: Properties of Matter
seo_title: Grade 5 Science: Properties of Matter Worksheets (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe the properties of solids, liquids and gases using the particle theory; describe changes of state; identify properties of materials and how they determine their uses. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand C: Matter and Energy – Properties of and Changes in Matter)
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 science worksheets on solids, liquids and gases, particles, changes of state and properties of materials. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Matter has mass and takes up space.
key_sub: Solids keep their shape, liquids take the shape of their container, and gases fill it.
body_html:
How to think about it

All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving.

  • Solid: particles packed tightly, fixed shape. Liquid: particles slide past each other. Gas: particles far apart and fast.
  • Heating makes particles move faster: melting, evaporation, sublimation. Cooling: freezing, condensation, deposition.
  • Properties like hardness, flexibility, conductivity and magnetism decide what a material is used for.
Example

Water vapour forms drops on a cold window. What change is this?

gas → liquid

Answer: condensation

Example

When ice melts, does its mass change?

the particles are the same

Answer: no

Common mistakes

  • Thinking air is not matter.
  • Mixing up evaporation and condensation.
  • Thinking mass changes when something melts.

faq.q: What are the three states of matter?
faq.a: Solid, liquid and gas. They differ in how closely packed the particles are and how they move.
A solid turning straight into a gas, like snow disappearing on a cold sunny day or dry ice.
Air has mass and takes up space, so it is matter even though we cannot see it.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Which property can you measure with a balance?
items.e: A balance compares masses.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid?
items.e: A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid?
items.e: A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: Which state of matter takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume?
items.e: Liquids flow.

items.q: Which state of matter escapes from an open container?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: What is it called when a liquid turns into a gas?
items.e: Puddles dry up by evaporation.

items.q: Is a coin a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: A coin is a solid.

items.q: Is helium in a balloon a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Helium in a balloon is a gas.

items.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Which of these is a solid?
items.e: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.

items.q: Is salt a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Salt grains are tiny solids.

items.q: What is it called when a solid turns directly into a gas?
items.e: Dry ice sublimes.

items.q: Is carbon dioxide a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: Is the air inside a soccer ball a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: The air inside a soccer ball is a gas.

items.q: Is shampoo a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Shampoo is a liquid.

items.q: Is water a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Water is a liquid.

items.q: Is orange juice a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: Snow disappears on a sunny winter day without melting. What happened?
c: It sublimated, turning straight into water vapour.
items.e: Sublimation skips the liquid state.

items.q: Which state of matter has a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
items.e: Solids keep their shape.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a liquid?
c: close together but able to slide past each other
packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
far apart and moving quickly in all directions
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Which state of matter does the model show?
items.e: In a gas the particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Orange juice has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: A rainbow has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. A rock is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: In which state are the particles far apart and moving quickly in all directions?
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: In which state are the particles packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot?
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Which property describes how easily a material bends without breaking?
items.e: Rubber is flexible.

items.q: Which state of matter does the model show?
items.e: In a solid the particles are packed tightly in a pattern and only vibrate in place.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: Heat has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. A pencil is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: The light from a lamp has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. The helium in a balloon is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: Look at how close the particles are. Which state of matter is this?
items.e: In a solid the particles are packed tightly in a pattern and only vibrate in place.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: A sound has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. Water vapour is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Air has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: A rock has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
items.e: Gas particles move freely.

items.q: Look at how close the particles are. Which state of matter is this?
items.e: In a liquid the particles touch, but they are not in rows and they slide past each other.

items.q: What state of matter is a mystery material in, according to this model?
items.e: In a liquid the particles touch, but they are not in rows and they slide past each other.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a gas?
c: far apart and moving quickly in all directions
close together but able to slide past each other
packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Water vapour has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Steam has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which word describes a liquid changing into a solid?
items.e: Melting, freezing, evaporating (and boiling), condensing.

items.q: Why is a stainless steel pot good for cooking?
c: It conducts heat well and does not melt on the stove.
items.e: Material choice depends on properties.

items.q: A toilet mirror mists up after a shower. Which change of state is this?
items.e: Is it getting hotter or colder? Which state does it start and end in?

a solid changing into a liquid when it is heated
a gas changing into a liquid when it is cooled

items.q: Water droplets form on a cold can of drink. Which change of state is this?
items.e: Is it getting hotter or colder? Which state does it start and end in?

items.q: Why is a winter coat filled with feathers or polyester fibres?
c: They trap air, which is a good insulator.
items.e: Trapped air slows heat loss.

items.q: Melted candle wax drips and goes hard again. Which change of state is this?
items.e: Is it getting hotter or colder? Which state does it start and end in?

items.q: When ice melts, what happens to its mass?
items.e: Changes of state do not change mass.

items.q: Which object is an electrical insulator?
items.e: A paper cup does not let electricity flow through it. All the other objects are metals, which are conductors.

items.q: Which object will a magnet pick up?
items.e: A steel washer contains iron, so it is attracted to a magnet. Many metals, like aluminum, copper and gold, are not.

items.q: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which object placed across the gap will make the bulb light?
items.e: Metals conduct electricity. A paper cup is an insulator.

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Small pebbles does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Pepper does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: Benjamin puts a sample on a balance. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's mass.

items.q: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which object placed across the gap will make the bulb light?
items.e: Metals conduct electricity. A glass marble is an insulator.

items.q: Which metal object will not stick to a magnet?
items.e: A copper wire is a metal, but it has no iron in it, so a magnet does not attract it. Iron and steel are attracted to magnets.

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Cornstarch does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: Chloe tries to scratch a mineral with a steel nail. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's hardness.

items.q: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which object placed across the gap will make the bulb light?
items.e: Metals conduct electricity. A cotton ball is an insulator.

items.q: Liam rubs a metal coin and watches it shine under a lamp. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's reflectivity.

items.q: Maya shines a flashlight on a rock to see if it sparkles. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's reflectivity.

items.q: Which metal object will not stick to a magnet?
items.e: A brass key is a metal, but it has no iron in it, so a magnet does not attract it. Iron and steel are attracted to magnets.

items.q: Zoe puts a sample on a balance. Which property is she testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's mass.

items.q: Which of these dissolves in water?
items.e: Baking soda dissolves: it breaks into particles too small to see and spreads through the water.

items.q: Which of these does not dissolve in water?
items.e: Chalk dust does not dissolve. You can still see it in the water, or it settles to the bottom.

items.q: Which object will a magnet pick up?
items.e: Iron filings contains iron, so it is attracted to a magnet. Many metals, like aluminum, copper and gold, are not.

items.q: A bulb is in a circuit with a gap. Which object placed across the gap will make the bulb light?
items.e: Graphite is not a metal, but it does conduct electricity. A rubber eraser is an insulator.

items.q: Ethan drops a sugar cube into warm tea and waits. Which property is he testing?
items.e: This test shows the material's solubility.

items.q: Lucas sorts 10 objects into “attracted to a magnet” and “not attracted.” Which conclusion is supported?
c: All attracted objects contain iron or steel, but not all metals are attracted.
items.e: Some metals, like aluminum and copper, end up in the “not attracted” group.

items.q: Ethan blows up two balloons the same size. He puts one in a warm room and one outside on a cold night. What happens to the outside balloon?
items.e: Cooling makes the air particles move more slowly and take up less space.

items.q: A flat ball has a mass of 544 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 555 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 555 − 544 = 11 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: A flat bike tire has a mass of 452 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 462 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 462 − 452 = 10 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

c: Gas particles move and spread out in all directions.

items.e: Gas particles move freely.

items.q: Noah wraps an ice cube in a bag, seals it and weighs it: 25 g. He weighs it again after it melts. What should the scale show?
items.e: Melting does not add or remove particles. The water has the same mass as the ice: 25 g.

items.q: Emma fills a plastic bottle with hot air, caps it and puts it in the freezer. The next day the bottle is dented in. Which model explains this?
c: Air particles were destroyed by the cold.
The cooled air particles slowed down and pushed less on the inside of the bottle.
items.e: Cold air particles move more slowly. They push less on the walls, so the air outside dents the bottle.

items.q: Sofia's mystery liquid freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. Which liquid is it most likely?
items.e: Pure water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. The temperatures where a substance changes state help identify it.

items.q: A flat soccer ball has a mass of 410 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 421 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 421 − 410 = 11 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: A sponge gets smaller when squeezed. Does this mean solids can be squashed?
c: No. The air in the holes is squeezed out; the solid itself does not shrink.
Yes, all solids can be squashed.
items.e: Think about what is in the holes.

items.q: Why is toothpaste hard to classify?
c: It holds its shape a little but flows when squeezed, so it has properties of solids and liquids.
items.e: Some materials are tricky.

items.q: Students test which material keeps ice frozen longest: foil, wool or plastic wrap. The ice in wool lasts longest. What does this show?
c: Wool is the best conductor of heat.
Wool is the best thermal insulator of the three.
items.e: Wool slows the movement of heat from the air to the ice, so the ice melts more slowly.

items.q: Ethan notices that a bicycle tire looks a little flat on a cold morning and fuller on a hot afternoon. No air was added. Why?
c: Warm air particles move faster and push harder on the tire.
The tire made more air during the day.
items.e: The same air is inside. When it warms, the particles move faster and push outward more.
